newsitem.title: ALBANIA: UNHCR recommends no action on fleeing Albanians.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR recommends no action on fleeing Albanians.

text.p: The flood of Albanians trying to flee their homeland continues unabated and a U.N. refugee official on Saturday recommended no action against them until after a general election.

Thousands of Albanians have fled across the Adriatic to Italy or over the southern border into Greece since a wave of violence broke across the small Balkan nation three months ago when popular, high-risk savings funds collapsed.

Although the main reasons for the exodus appeared to be economic or to escape the armed gangs now terrorising southern Albania, the U.N. official said there was a political element that could lead to harrassment if people were sent back.

"I would recommend that host countries take no action against Albanians until after the general election (expected on June 29)," Olivier Guignabaudet, on a mission in Albania for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), told Reuters.
"It is better to resolve the conflict through the ballot box rather than through bullets.

"Allow these people to remain on temporary residency... then after the election the international community can draw its conclusion. Starting to think about a return programme now is, in my view, premature."
This is the second time that large numbers of people from Europe's poorest nation have fled their homeland.
A huge number of Albanians emigrated illegally to Italy and Greece in 1991 and 1992 after the collapse of the ruthless Stalinist government which ruled for 46 years.
On March 1 this year, Albania's Democratic Party government was forced to resign as angry Albanians took to the streets to protest about the collapsed savings schemes.
President Sali Berisha, who has ruled since 1992, appointed an interim all-party government and agreed to call an election, four years early, to restore faith in the government.

While the Democrats and opposition Socialists struggle to agree on election laws, the international community is urging the election takes place in June and a multi-national force has been deployed in Albania to oversee aid deliveries.
Guignabaudet recommended countries housing illegal immigrants could implement a return-to-vote programme, encouraging Albanians to return home voluntarily to vote.
Meanwhile the number of Albanians seeking to flee continues -- earning thousands of dollars for smugglers exploiting the situation but with some tragic consequences.

An estimated 103 people drowned on March 28 when an ship from Vlore in southern Albania collided with an Italian navy frigate 30 miles off Brindisi in southern Italy. The passengers paid $500 each for a space on the boat.

A week ago Italian authorities at Badetta rescued 571 Albanians crammed into a vessel built for 50 that left from Velipoje Beach, 30 kms from Shkoder in northern Albania. Italy has returned 267 of these people, local news agency ATA said.
In recent days 4,000 people have been camped out near Velipoje, hoping to leave for Italy but have been prevented by Italian navy vessels patrolling the coast.
Guignabaudet said economic reasons undoubtedly caused many Albanians to leave, as during 1991/92.
"But these economic conditions have always existed. At both times of these mass departures, critical political changes have taken place," he said.
